newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU prepares for delay in treaty talks.
newsitem.headline: EU prepares for delay in treaty talks.

text.p: Britain's forthcoming general election and questions about the European stance of a new government in London have forced the European Union to prepare for a delay in its treaty negotiations.
Such a move risks slowing whatever momentum has been building in the inter-governmental conference (IGC) and putting off the formal start of enlargement talks with eastern Europe.
Luxembourg said on Monday that it was reserving two days during its EU presidency in the second half of this year for special summits at which a new treaty could be agreed.
The Grand Duchy takes over the EU presidency from the Netherlands on July 1, two weeks after the European Council in Amsterdam is supposed to wrap up the IGC.
"There are two possible dates, in July or October," Luxembourg government press officer Guy Schuller told Reuters, confirming a report in the Luxembourger Wort newspaper.
He said the dates were July 25 and October 10.

Although Schuller noted that setting the dates for special summits was purely contingency planning, the move underlines the growing belief in EU capitals that the bloc will not be able to end the talks in Amsterdam on June 16-17 as planned.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television aired on Monday, Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said: "I strongly hope the Dutch will (complete the IGC) but it is not a disaster if there is no agreement."

A delay, however, would be significant as it would both open the door psychologically to further delays and could put back the start of formal negotiations with applicant countries from eastern Europe and the Mediterranean.

Enlargement talks with as many as 11 countries are scheduled to begin six months after the end of the treaty negotiations. The IGC was called in part to prepare the bloc for such a large influx of members.

Senior Dutch officials admitted privately at the start of their presidency this month that although they would like to bring the talks to a close on the Netherlands' watch, there is a working assumption that the end of the IGC will have to be put off.

The reason is Britain, where Prime Minister John Major's government opposes many of the proposals under discussion in the IGC. Major must hold an election by May 22, but is considered likely to go for one on May 1.
That would leave only six weeks for the winner -- expected to be Tony Blair's Labour Party -- to set up in office and to become formally immersed in the negotiations.
"I am fully aware of the risks and uncertainties...including the uncertainty related to the upcoming British elections," Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said last week.

The Dutch, who have expressed concern that an anti-EU campaign leading up to the election may make it difficult for any British government to make needed compromises, accept that six weeks is probably too short a time.
Kok said he hoped the British election would be called as soon as possible -- whoever the likely winner.
One of Kok's first moves on taking over the EU presidency was to meet Major in The Hague to encourage the British prime minister not to allow his elections to disrupt the planned treaty.
